subject: N-method hotspot analysis for DO mice

messages.author: 1504d994a3b46924
messages.subject: N-method hotspot analysis for DO mice
parts:
Hello, 

My lab is interested in using the N-method of identifying hotspots in a DO mouse QTL study. 

Some Background: 
  • Brian Yandell has already made the 'qtlhot' package, which accepts cross1 objects and performs permutation scans with the goal of creating an empirical null distribution of maxmimum hotspot sizes at any given locus.   
  • r/qtl2 has allowed us to analyze DO mice by accepting a kinship matrix and using a LMM approach. The cross2 object that facilitates this is, unfortunately, incompatible with qtlhot. 
Our Goal:
  • Using a research cluster, we would like to create our own null distribution of max hotspot sizes for a DO mouse study by permuting the rows of the apr object across 1,000 scans of our MegaMUGA genotypes against our gene expression phenotype array. Following the N-method, each scan1 output would be subset for all eQTLs within a 1.8 LOD drop interval of the peaks. The subset will be filtered at the GWER threshold, and the maximum number of the remaining eQTLs on a single locus will be recorded. 
Our Questions/Concerns:
  • Our initial premise was based off this line in the scan1perm() documentation: 
    • If kinship is provided, we instead permute the rows of the genotype data and fit an LMM with the same residual heritability (estimated under the null hypothesis of no QTL).
    • We thought that if a threshold for controlling genome-wide error could be generated using this method, we could create valid permutations for hotspot analysis. 
    • However, we are unsure of the underlined portion - does this refer to the kinship matrix? Does this mean we only permute the apr rows and do not have to touch the kinship matrix across permutations? 
  • Finally, we would like general feedback as to whether permutation of LMM DO mouse scans would create a valid null distribution.
Thank you for your time, 

Excel

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] N-method hotspot analysis for DO mice
parts:
This is one of the approaches considered by Cheng and Palmer (2013) https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.112.146332

You permute the rows of the genotype data, and keep the phenotype data and kinship matrix intact, and so the estimated residual heritability will be the same because it's calculated using just the phenotypes and kinship, and not the genotypes.

It's believed to control the false positive rate, but it's not entirely clear why. There has been no formal proof, or theory to back it up; it just works in simulation studies, and the permutation thresholds obtained seem reasonable.

If it works for one trait, it should work for a set of them.

karl
